questions.section: Section A: Real Numbers and Algebra
questions.stem: A dimensionless calibration setting \(x\) is adjusted during a bench test. The same test also uses a small error parameter \(\epsilon\) and a sequence of linearly increasing readings.
questions.title: Calibration algebra and finite sums

parts.answer:
First solve the two inequalities separately. For
\[
\frac{2x-1}{x+2}>0,
\]
the critical values are \(x=-2\) and \(x=\frac{1}{2}\). A sign chart gives \(x<-2\) or \(x>\frac{1}{2}\). Next,
\[
\frac{2x-1}{x+2}<1
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\frac{2x-1-(x+2)}{x+2}<0,
\]
so
\[
\frac{x-3}{x+2}<0.
\]
This holds for \(-2<x<3\). Intersecting the two conditions gives
\[
\frac{1}{2}<x<3.
\]
parts.label: (a)

parts.answer:
Using the binomial theorem,
\[
(1+2\epsilon)^5=1+5(2\epsilon)+10(2\epsilon)^2+10(2\epsilon)^3+5(2\epsilon)^4+(2\epsilon)^5.
\]
Keeping terms up to \(\epsilon^3\),
\[
(1+2\epsilon)^5\approx 1+10\epsilon+40\epsilon^2+80\epsilon^3.
\]
For \(\epsilon=0.01\),
\[
1+10(0.01)+40(0.01)^2+80(0.01)^3=1.10408.
\]
The cubic approximation is \(1.10408\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Expand \((1+2\epsilon)^5\) up to and including the term in \(\epsilon^3\). Use this to estimate \((1.02)^5\).

parts.answer:
Use the standard sums:
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-1)=4\sum_{r=1}^{n}r-\sum_{r=1}^{n}1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-1)=4\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}-n=2n(n+1)-n.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-1)=2n^2+n.
\]
If the sum is \(171\), then
\[
2n^2+n=171.
\]
Hence
\[
2n^2+n-171=0=(n-9)(2n+19).
\]
Since \(n\) is positive, \(n=9\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-1)\). Hence find \(n\) if this sum is \(171\).

questions.stem: An oscillatory signal is modelled by \(s(t)=4\sin t+3\cos t\), where \(t\) is measured in radians. A separate small-angle calculation is used to compare two nearby signals.
questions.title: Oscillatory signal model

parts.answer:
Write
\[
4\sin t+3\cos t=5\sin(t+\alpha).
\]
Expanding the right-hand side gives
\[
5\sin(t+\alpha)=5\sin t\cos\alpha+5\cos t\sin\alpha.
\]
Comparing coefficients,
\[
5\cos\alpha=4,\qquad 5\sin\alpha=3.
\]
Thus
\[
\cos\alpha=\frac{4}{5},\qquad \sin\alpha=\frac{3}{5},\qquad \alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
s(t)=5\sin\left(t+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\right).
\]
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write \(s(t)=4\sin t+3\cos t\) in the form \(R\sin(t+\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.answer:
From part (a),
\[
s(t)=5\sin(t+\alpha),\qquad \alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right).
\]
The maximum value of the sine function is \(1\), so the maximum signal value is \(5\). This first occurs when
\[
t+\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
t=\frac{\pi}{2}-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right).
\]
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the maximum value of \(s(t)\), and find the first \(t\) in \([0,2\pi)\) at which it occurs.

parts.answer:
Separate the two sine terms:
\[
\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin(5u)-\sin(2u)}{u}=\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin(5u)}{u}-\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin(2u)}{u}.
\]
For the first term,
\[
\frac{\sin(5u)}{u}=5\frac{\sin(5u)}{5u}\to5.
\]
For the second term,
\[
\frac{\sin(2u)}{u}=2\frac{\sin(2u)}{2u}\to2.
\]
Therefore the limit is
\[
5-2=3.
\]
parts.label: (c)

questions.stem: A displacement model for a short pulse is \(x(t)=t^2e^{-t}\), where \(t\ge0\). A related accumulated work calculation uses a rational force model.
questions.title: Pulse rates and accumulated work

parts.answer:
Differentiate using the product rule:
\[
x'(t)=2t e^{-t}+t^2(-e^{-t}).
\]
Hence
\[
x'(t)=e^{-t}(2t-t^2)=t(2-t)e^{-t}.
\]
For \(t>0\), the stationary point occurs when
\[
t(2-t)e^{-t}=0.
\]
Since \(e^{-t}\ne0\) and \(t>0\), the stationary time is
\[
t=2.
\]
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Differentiate \(x(t)=t^2e^{-t}\), and find the stationary time for \(t>0\).

parts.answer:
Use integration by parts with \(u=t\) and \(dv=e^{-t}\,dt\). Then \(du=dt\) and \(v=-e^{-t}\). Thus
\[
\int_0^2 t e^{-t}\,dt=\left[-t e^{-t}\right]_0^2+\int_0^2 e^{-t}\,dt.
\]
Now
\[
\left[-t e^{-t}\right]_0^2=-2e^{-2}
\]
and
\[
\int_0^2 e^{-t}\,dt=\left[-e^{-t}\right]_0^2=1-e^{-2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_0^2 t e^{-t}\,dt=1-3e^{-2}.
\]
parts.label: (b)

parts.answer:
Factor the denominator:
\[
x^2+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2).
\]
Let
\[
\frac{3x+5}{x^2+3x+2}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+2}.
\]
Then
\[
3x+5=A(x+2)+B(x+1).
\]
Comparing coefficients gives
\[
A+B=3,\qquad 2A+B=5.
\]
Thus \(A=2\) and \(B=1\). Hence
\[
\int_0^1\frac{3x+5}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx=\int_0^1\left(\frac{2}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx.
\]
So
\[
\left[2\ln(x+1)+\ln(x+2)\right]_0^1=2\ln2+\ln3-\ln2=\ln6.
\]
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Resolve \(\frac{3x+5}{x^2+3x+2}\) into partial fractions, and evaluate \(\int_0^1\frac{3x+5}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx\).

questions.stem: A phasor has complex amplitude \(z=\sqrt{3}+i\). Complex roots are used to describe equally spaced phase choices.
questions.title: Phasors and roots

parts.answer:
The modulus is
\[
|z|=\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+1^2}=2.
\]
The argument is
\[
\arg z=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6},
\]
since \(z\) lies in the first quadrant. Therefore
\[
z=2e^{i\pi/6}.
\]
By De Moivre's theorem,
\[
z^6=2^6e^{i\pi}=-64.
\]
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write \(z=\sqrt{3}+i\) in exponential form, and hence find \(z^6\).

parts.answer:
Since
\[
z=2e^{i\pi/6},
\]
the cube roots have modulus \(2^{1/3}\). Their arguments are
\[
\frac{\frac{\pi}{6}+2k\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{18}+\frac{2k\pi}{3},\qquad k=0,1,2.
\]
Therefore
\[
w=2^{1/3}e^{i(\pi/18+2k\pi/3)},\qquad k=0,1,2.
\]
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the three cube roots of \(z\), giving your answers in exponential form.

parts.answer:
Use Euler form term by term:
\[
2e^{i\pi/3}=2\left(\frac{1}{2}+i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=1+i\sqrt{3}.
\]
Also,
\[
3e^{-i\pi/6}=3\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-i\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{3i}{2}.
\]
Adding gives
\[
A=1+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}+i\left(\sqrt{3}-\frac{3}{2}\right).
\]
The real part is \(1+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and the imaginary part is \(\sqrt{3}-\frac{3}{2}\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Let \(A=2e^{i\pi/3}+3e^{-i\pi/6}\). Find the real and imaginary parts of \(A\).
